question.problem:
Solve the modular equation $4x≡7\,(\text{mod}\,11).$ 

*Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.*
question.worked_solution:
Recall that a linear congruence $ax≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and only if $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

In the given congruence, we have $a=4$ and $n=11$, and

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(4,11)=1.
$$

So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $4\,(\text{mod}\,11).$ To find the inverse of $4\,(\text{mod}\,11)$, we compute the exponents of $4\,(\text{mod}\,11)$ until we get a result of $1\,(\text{mod}\,11):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{2} & ≡16≡5 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ {4}^{3} & ≡5\cdot 4≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ {4}^{4} & ≡9\cdot 4≡3 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ {4}^{5} & ≡3\cdot 4≡12≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,11)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $3\cdot 4≡1\,(\text{mod}\,11),$ which means that $3$ is the multiplicative inverse of $4$ (modulo $11$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $3,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & ≡7 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ 3\cdot 4x & ≡3\cdot 7 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ (3\cdot 4)x & ≡21 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ 1\cdot x & ≡1\cdot 11+10 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ x & ≡10 &  & (\text{mod}\,11)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x≡10\,(\text{mod}\,11).$
